question: A patient receives a sedative medication right before intubation and suddenly becomes very dizzy with a dangerous drop in blood pressure. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: The bag-valve-mask was squeezed too hard during manual ventilation
options.B: The patient was not breathing enough oxygen before the procedure started
options.C: Many induction drugs cause blood vessels to relax and lower blood pressure
options.D: The endotracheal tube was inserted too deeply into the right mainstem bronchus

explanation: Sedatives and induction agents frequently cause vasodilation, which can drop blood pressure sharply, particularly in unstable patients. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h3)

question: Why must nurses look at published research with a critical eye?

options.A: Research studies are only meant for academic promotion
options.B: Hospital management requires nurses to rewrite journal articles
options.C: Authors purposely hide their results to confuse readers
options.D: Not all published studies are designed or conducted well

explanation: Even peer-reviewed journals can contain flaws, so nurses must evaluate the evidence before applying it to patients. [learn more](GNS224_U4_T4#GNS224_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical problem caused by untreated anosmia?

options.A: Danger of failing to detect smoke or gas leaks
options.B: Inability to hear high-pitched vocal tones
options.C: Decreased appetite and unintended weight loss
options.D: Distorted enjoyment of food due to lost flavor

explanation: You got it! Hearing is handled by auditory pathways in the temporal lobe, not the nose. Smell loss won't affect how well you hear high notes. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h7)

question: What do we mean by 'patient harm' in a healthcare setting?

options.A: Injury caused by medical care rather than the underlying disease
options.B: Emotional distress caused by a patient's personal family issues
options.C: Discomfort experienced before a formal diagnosis is made
options.D: Natural progression of a chronic illness over time

explanation: Spot on! Patient harm refers specifically to injuries that happen because of the medical care or treatment provided, rather than the natural course of the sickness itself. Keep up the great thinking! [learn more](GNS312_U5_T6#GNS312_U5_T6_h1)

question: What happens inside your chest when your diaphragm contracts to take in a normal breath?

options.A: Surface tension increases to make the lung tissue stiffer
options.B: Intrapleural pressure decreases to draw air into the lungs
options.C: Intrapleural pressure increases to force air out of the lungs
options.D: The chest wall pushes inward to compress the lung tissue

explanation: Great thinking! When your diaphragm moves down and your chest expands, the pressure inside drops below the outside air pressure, naturally sucking air in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h1)

question: How does fluid in the chest cavity (pleural effusion) make it hard to breathe?

options.A: Fluid enters the alveoli and destroys the natural surfactant
options.B: It blocks the main windpipe and chugs off air supply
options.C: Fluid physically presses against the lung, stopping it from expanding fully
options.D: It forces the heart to beat too fast, causing sudden shock

explanation: You got it! The fluid takes up space in the chest and squeezes the lung from the outside, so it can't puff up nicely when breathing in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h4)

question: If one person in a house has scabies, why is it super important to treat everyone living in that home at the same time?

options.A: Mites spread easily through close personal contact and shared bedding
options.B: Topical creams expire quickly once opened in a shared household
options.C: Family members always develop symptoms faster than the index patient
options.D: Untreated family members will develop permanent skin scarring

explanation: Scabies mites love to hop between people through skin contact or shared blankets. Treating the whole household at once stops everyone from passing the bugs back and forth! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h5)

question: You notice your clinic frequently runs out of single-use syringes, causing staff to reuse equipment. What is your best professional action?

options.A: Keep quiet so you don't upset the clinic manager during a busy shift
options.B: Buy plastic syringes from a local pharmacy using your own money
options.C: Stop giving all prescribed medications until the hospital closes
options.D: Report the shortage through official channels and advocate for safer supplies

explanation: Spot on! As a nurse, you have a duty to advocate for your patients and push for proper resources when safety is on the line. Great clinical leadership! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h9)

question: What is a major long-term health problem linked to chronic Hepatitis C caught from unsafe injections?

options.A: Rapid weakening of the leg muscles
options.B: Permanent loss of hearing and balance
options.C: Chronic respiratory failure and asthma
options.D: Cirrhosis and severe liver damage

explanation: Hepatitis C quietly attacks the liver over many years, leading to scarring (cirrhosis) and raising the risk of liver cancer. This is why our injection technique matters so much! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h5)

question: How do dendrites differ in function from axons?

options.A: Dendrites are found only in the brain, while axons are in the spinal cord
options.B: Dendrites carry signals toward the cell body, while axons carry them away
options.C: Dendrites produce myelin, while axons produce neurotransmitters
options.D: Dendrites control voluntary movement, while axons control involuntary actions

explanation: Dendrites act as receiving antennas, whereas axons transmit the nerve impulse outward to other cells. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why can relying completely on international donors be risky for a hospital's Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: International agencies refuse to supply common medicines like antibiotics
options.B: Donor drugs are always expired before they arrive at the hospital
options.C: Local nurses are legally forbidden from handling donated medical items
options.D: Donor programs can end or shift priorities abruptly, causing shortages

explanation: Right! External aid can disappear overnight. If you don't have a local system making money to buy drugs, you'll run out fast when donors leave. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which part of the nail is responsible for growing new nail cells?

options.A: The nail plate
options.B: The nail matrix
options.C: The cuticle
options.D: The nail bed

explanation: Great job! The nail matrix sits right under the skin at the base and does all the hard work of making new cells that push forward to form your hard nails. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T4#GNS112_U5_T4_h1)

question: What is the medical term for the crunching sound when broken bone ends rub together?

options.A: Cyanosis
options.B: Crepitus
options.C: Contracture
options.D: Clonus

explanation: Crepitus is that distinct crunching sound or feeling you get when jagged ends of a broken bone grind against each other. It's a classic sign nurses listen and feel for during assessments! [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h3)

question: What does the acronym PMTCT stand for in healthcare?

options.A: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission
options.B: Post-Mortem Tissue and Cell Testing
options.C: Primary Medical Treatment and Care Techniques
options.D: Pediatric Management of Therapeutic Care and Treatment

explanation: PMTCT is a global public health strategy specifically designed to stop the transmission of HIV from mothers to their babies during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h1)

question: What does the ethical principle of autonomy mean for an older patient?

options.A: The duty of the nurse to do no harm
options.B: The obligation to tell the truth at all times
options.C: The fair distribution of medical resources
options.D: The right to make their own healthcare decisions

explanation: Autonomy refers to a person's independence and right to self-determination regarding their medical care. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T1#GNS321_U3_T1_h6)

question: How is gender expression different from gender identity?

options.A: Expression is the outward display of gender, while identity is the internal feeling
options.B: Expression has no connection to societal rules, unlike identity
options.C: Expression is fixed at birth, while identity changes daily
options.D: Expression refers only to chromosomes, while identity refers to hormones

explanation: Exactly right! Gender expression is what others can see (like clothing and behavior), whereas gender identity is a private, internal experience. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T2#GNS312_U4_T2_h2)

question: What are unexplained fevers, night sweats, and weight loss in lymphoma called?

options.A: B symptoms
options.B: Metabolic syndrome
options.C: Constitutional markers
options.D: A symptoms

explanation: In clinical practice, we group these classic warning signs—fever, drenching night sweats, and weight loss—together as 'B symptoms'. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the primary danger of untreated prolonged obstructed labor?

options.A: Postpartum hair loss
options.B: Obstetric fistula
options.C: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.D: Gestational diabetes

explanation: Prolonged pressure from the baby's head cuts off blood supply to surrounding tissues, causing necrosis and leading to abnormal holes between the vagina and bladder or rectum. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h3)

question: What anatomical feature of the skin creates your unique fingerprints?

options.A: Dermal papillae interlocking beneath the surface
options.B: Friction of the outer skin rubbing against clothes
options.C: Sweat gland tubes branching out
options.D: Adipose tissue buildup in the lower layer

explanation: You got it! Tiny wave-like bumps called dermal papillae push up from the dermis, creating the unique patterns we know as fingerprints. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h3)

question: What vital document must a nurse provide when sending a client to another facility?

options.A: A receipt for the purchase of family planning drugs
options.B: A discharge certificate from the local government
options.C: A blank prescription sheet signed by the patient
options.D: A completed and legible referral form

explanation: A formal referral form communicates the clinical history and reason for transfer directly to the receiving healthcare providers. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T029#GNS226_U6_T029_h5)

question: What is the most effective way for a nurse to interview a suspected victim of breast ironing?

options.A: In a busy hospital hallway in front of other visitors
options.B: By asking the mother to explain all the child's injuries
options.C: By waiting until the doctor completes a full physical exam
options.D: In a private room away from accompanying family members

explanation: Privacy is essential because accompanying relatives are often the perpetrators or supporters of the abuse. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T17#GNS312_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is the main job of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the kidneys?

options.A: Stimulating the excretion of excess water in urine
options.B: Blocking the reabsorption of sodium ions
options.C: Promoting water reabsorption into the blood
options.D: Increasing the production of red blood cells

explanation: Think of ADH as your body's water-saver. When you're running low on fluids, ADH tells your kidneys to hold onto water and put it back into your bloodstream. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h4)

question: How does gastroenteritis fundamentally affect the gastrointestinal tract?

options.A: It blocks the bile ducts and stops liver enzyme production
options.B: It creates permanent ulcers in the lower esophageal sphincter
options.C: It permanently destroys the muscular wall of the large bowel
options.D: It causes inflammation of the stomach and intestinal lining

explanation: The core pathological feature of gastroenteritis is the acute inflammation of the mucous membranes inside the stomach and intestines. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h1)

question: How should you talk to a parent who is scared about vaccines because of community rumors?

options.A: Tell the parent that asking questions about modern medicine is illegal
options.B: Scold the parent publicly to discourage other community members from doubting
options.C: Listen respectfully, validate their concerns, and provide clear factual explanations
options.D: Ignore the questions entirely and administer the injections without speaking

explanation: As a nurse, patience is key. Listening without judgment and sharing gentle, honest facts builds trust way faster than arguing. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h7)

question: What is the main benefit of involving local residents in data collection?

options.A: It allows nurses to stay inside the office all day long
options.B: It builds local ownership and trust in health programs
options.C: It forces community members to pay taxes to the clinic
options.D: It removes the need for professional nursing training

explanation: When residents participate in the diagnostic process, they value the resulting health interventions and support them willingly. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T3#GNS124_U3_T3_h4)

question: A patient taking ED meds is prescribed nitroglycerin for chest pain. What is your most critical nursing action?

options.A: Encourage the patient to ignore the chest pain
options.B: Tell the patient to stop taking all physical exercise
options.C: Warn the patient about the fatal drop in blood pressure
options.D: Advise the patient to double their water intake daily

explanation: Crucial nursing catch! This is a textbook dangerous drug interaction that can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension. Always educate your patient! [learn more](GNS312_U1_T24#GNS312_U1_T24_h8)

question: What is an important way nurses can guide patients and visitors regarding ward waste?

options.A: Revising the hospital's annual financial budget
options.B: Teaching them how to operate surgical autoclaves
options.C: Explaining the correct use of color-coded waste bins
options.D: Training them to administer intravenous injections

explanation: Visitors often toss things into the nearest bin. Taking a second to guide them helps keep our color-coded waste streams pure! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T17#GNS122_U3_T17_h6)

question: What are the three main functions of the nervous system?

options.A: Digestion, absorption, and elimination
options.B: Sensory input, integration, and motor output
options.C: Protection, support, and movement
options.D: Circulation, respiration, and excretion

explanation: The nervous system constantly gathers information, processes it in the brain and spinal cord, and sends out commands to the body. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the main goal of rehabilitation in nursing care?

options.A: To completely cure chronic underlying pathologies
options.B: To eliminate the need for any follow-up care
options.C: To maximize a person's independence and functional level
options.D: To keep patients admitted in hospital wards long-term

explanation: You've got this! Rehab is all about helping your patients live life to the fullest and do as much for themselves as possible, even if a chronic condition is still there. [learn more](GNS123_U6_T6#GNS123_U6_T6_h1)

question: What is the main goal of performing a pleurodesis via the intrapleural route?

options.A: To dissolve blood clots located inside the heart chambers
options.B: To deliver systemic antibiotics for a urinary infection
options.C: To obliterate the pleural space and prevent fluid return
options.D: To permanently dilate the main bronchial airways

explanation: Well done! Pleurodesis creates a controlled scar that seals the pleural space shut, stopping stubborn fluid or air from coming back. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T12#GNS125_U3_T12_h3)

question: What is the absolute gold standard method to confirm an NG tube is sitting correctly?

options.A: Abdominal X-ray confirmation
options.B: Auscultating an air bolus over the stomach
options.C: Observing condensation inside the clear plastic tube
options.D: Checking if the patient can speak clearly

explanation: An X-ray never guesses! It gives you a clear picture of exactly where the tube tip is resting, making it the top gold standard. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which of these is a great non-drug way to handle behavioral symptoms in a patient?

options.A: Restricting all visits from family and close friends
options.B: Administering high doses of sedating antipsychotic drugs
options.C: Moving the patient to a completely unfamiliar location daily
options.D: Maintaining predictable daily routines in a calm environment

explanation: You got it! Calm settings and steady daily routines do wonders to soothe patients and lower anxiety without needing extra pills. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h5)

question: Why is teaching self-examination important in male reproductive care?

options.A: It is the only reliable way to diagnose a urinary tract infection
options.B: It replaces the need for any future professional medical visits
options.C: It helps patients detect early changes like lumps or swelling
options.D: It prevents the normal age-related decrease in testosterone

explanation: Correct! Self-exams empower patients to notice small changes right away, leading to quicker medical help and better health results. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which symptom is the earliest and most reliable indicator of developing compartment syndrome?

options.A: Complete lack of any pulse felt in the foot or hand
options.B: Blue discoloration of the skin spreading rapidly over the toes
options.C: Severe, relentless pain that is not relieved by opioid pain medication
options.D: Total paralysis of all the fingers and toes on the affected limb

explanation: Intense, out-of-proportion pain that fails to respond to strong painkillers is the hallmark early warning sign of rising pressure inside a muscle compartment. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h6)

question: In the tablet dosage formula, what does the 'Have' part stand for?

options.A: The total number of tablets remaining in the patient's drawer
options.B: The maximum daily limit prescribed for the patient
options.C: The strength of the medication available in stock
options.D: The exact dose requested by the medical officer

explanation: You got it! 'Have' is simply the strength written on the medicine package you currently have in your hand. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T6#GNS125_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why do many young women and teenagers in Nigeria end up turning to unsafe abortion methods?

options.A: Preference for traditional herbal remedies over modern medicine
options.B: Easy availability of safe surgical clinics in rural areas
options.C: Lack of financial resources and reproductive health access
options.D: Strict enforcement of mandatory hospital reporting laws

explanation: Poverty, fear of social stigma, and struggling to find safe, legal services often push vulnerable girls into dangerous alternatives. As nurses, keeping our clinics open and welcoming is key to changing this. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T026#GNS226_U5_T026_h1)

question: What does a high D-dimer blood test usually tell the healthcare team?

options.A: The body is actively forming and breaking down blood clots
options.B: The patient has a severe primary iron deficiency anemia
options.C: The bone marrow is producing too many immature white cells
options.D: There is a complete lack of red blood cell production

explanation: A D-dimer is essentially microscopic debris left behind when the body dissolves a clot. If it's high, it means clotting and clot-busting are happening somewhere in the body. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h6)

question: A patient is admitted to a hospice facility. What must they or their surrogate agree to regarding their treatment?

options.A: To participate in experimental clinical drug trials
options.B: To undergo aggressive physical rehabilitation daily
options.C: To stop curative treatments and focus on comfort
options.D: To transfer back to an acute care hospital weekly

explanation: Choosing hospice care means electing to forego curative therapies in favor of comfort-focused palliative management. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h3)

question: What is the best position to place a distressed, breathless patient into right away?

options.A: High Fowler's or sitting upright leaning forward
options.B: Left lateral recovery position
options.C: Flat on the back with legs elevated
options.D: Prone position with a pillow under the chest

explanation: Gravity is our friend here! Sitting upright helps pull the diaphragm down, making it much easier for the patient to draw a breath. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T13#GNS123_U3_T13_h6)

question: What happens during an 'ascending infection' in the female reproductive system?

options.A: Pathogens move upward from the vagina and cervix into the uterus and fallopian tubes
options.B: Viruses migrate from skin lesions down to the regional lymph nodes
options.C: Fungi multiply rapidly on the external vulva and travel to the bladder
options.D: Bacteria travel through the bloodstream directly to the heart valves

explanation: An ascending infection is just germs traveling upward—moving past the cervix and into the upper reproductive organs where they can cause serious trouble. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T2#GNS216_U5_T2_h2)

question: Why is it sometimes good if a deworming drug stays in the gut and isn't easily absorbed into the blood?

options.A: It ensures the drug travels directly to the brain tissues
options.B: It prevents the liver from metabolizing any medication
options.C: It reduces the need for patients to drink water
options.D: It keeps the medication concentration high inside the gut lumen

explanation: Makes sense, right? Keeping the drug right in the intestines means it hits the tummy-dwelling worms with full force! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T7#GNS223_U3_T7_h4)

question: A nurse is preparing to feed a patient via a PEG tube. What action should be performed first?

options.A: Flush the tube rapidly with 100 mL of cold water
options.B: Lie the patient completely flat to check the abdomen
options.C: Verify tube placement and assess bowel sounds
options.D: Attach the feeding bag and start the pump immediately

explanation: Safety checks like confirming tube position and ensuring active bowel sounds must always happen before introducing any fluid or formula. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h3)

question: A surgical instrument slips from your hand and lands partially on the edge of the instrument table tray. What should you do?

options.A: Consider the instrument contaminated and discard it immediately.
options.B: Wipe the instrument with an alcohol swab before using it again.
options.C: Inspect the instrument to see if it touched the floor.
options.D: Use the instrument quickly before air contaminants settle on it.

explanation: When in doubt, throw it out! Touching that unsterile edge means the tool is no longer safe for the sterile field. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T3#GNS123_U5_T3_h4)

question: How is 'low vision' best described in a clinical setting?

options.A: Total, permanent blindness with zero light perception
options.B: Vision loss that cannot be fully fixed with regular glasses, medicine, or surgery
options.C: A temporary blur from eye strain or tiredness
options.D: Simple nearsightedness that is easily corrected with prescription lenses

explanation: Low vision means standard glasses or medical treatments can't bring sight back to normal, even though the person still has some helpful vision left. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h8)

question: Why are nurses so important when pregnant women come in for prenatal services?

options.A: They are legally required to perform all surgical procedures during birth
options.B: They prescribe all medications independently of medical doctors
options.C: They diagnose genetic disorders without needing laboratory equipment
options.D: They serve as the primary contact to build trust and encourage hospital deliveries

explanation: You are often the very first person she talks to! Building that warm, trusting relationship makes her feel safe and much more likely to come back for a safe hospital delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T008#GNS226_U1_T008_h1)

question: What is the main difference between an 'illness' and a 'disease'?

options.A: Disease can be cured by nursing care, but illness requires surgery.
options.B: Illness is a subjective feeling of being unwell, while disease is a physical alteration in body function.
options.C: Illness is diagnosed by laboratory tests, while disease is felt by the patient.
options.D: Illness only affects mental stability, whereas disease strictly affects organs.

explanation: Think of it this way: disease is the actual physical problem happening inside the body, while illness is how the patient actually experiences and feels that problem. [learn more](GNS112_U1_T3#GNS112_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is your main job as the nurse while the doctor performs a thoracentesis?

options.A: Reading the final lab results before fluid collection
options.B: Inserting the drainage catheter into the pleural cavity
options.C: Administering general anesthesia through an IV line
options.D: Monitoring vital signs and watching for signs of distress

explanation: Exactly right! Your eyes are on the patient—keep a close check on their breathing, heart rate, and comfort while the fluid drains. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h4)

question: Why is vigorous drying with a warm, clean towel so important right after birth?

options.A: It replaces the need for a stethoscope
options.B: It helps you polish the baby's skin to spot bruises
options.C: It washes off the vernix caseosa much faster
options.D: It stimulates breathing reflexes and stops rapid heat loss

explanation: Drying a wet baby stops them from getting cold too fast, and the gentle rubbing is great touch stimulation to help them take that first big cry! [learn more](GNS225_U3_T10#GNS225_U3_T10_h7)

question: What does an epidemic curve show us?

options.A: The geographic map of roads leading to isolation centers
options.B: The number of new cases plotted against the time of symptom onset
options.C: The total number of healthcare workers on daily duty shifts
options.D: The financial cost of medical supplies used during the emergency

explanation: An epi curve is simply a graph showing how many people fell sick over time. Great practice for your exams! [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is the main role of a healthcare proxy or durable power of attorney?

options.A: To pay the patient's medical bills out of their personal bank account
options.B: To write the medical orders that the doctor must follow
options.C: To provide nursing care inside the patient's home
options.D: To make medical decisions when the patient loses capacity

explanation: A healthcare proxy is a designated person who speaks for the patient and makes treatment choices when the patient can no longer do so. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h3)

question: What is a major reason why people with very little money sometimes end up with unsafe abortion practices?

options.A: Excessive availability of trained doctors
options.B: Lack of interest in personal health matters
options.C: Abundance of free clinics in rural communities
options.D: Inability to afford safe and legal medical services

explanation: Exactly. When safe care costs too much, financial desperation pushes people toward dangerous alternatives. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T022#GNS226_U5_T022_h2)

question: A 14-year-old patient starts dressing and speaking just like a new group of friends. How should you as a nurse view this?

options.A: An indication of developmental delay in cognitive reasoning
options.B: Evidence of negative peer pressure that requires institutionalization
options.C: A sign of severe psychological personality splitting
options.D: A normal part of peer bonding and identity exploration

explanation: Fitting in with friends is a healthy part of growing up. They are just trying out different styles to see what feels right! [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is a major blind spot when nurses rely only on hospital clinic registers for family planning stats?

options.A: They are updated only once every ten years by international agencies
options.B: They are completely digital and impossible for nurses to read
options.C: They only record data from patients who experience severe surgical complications
options.D: They miss clients who obtain contraceptives from pharmacies or traditional sources

explanation: Clinic books only show the people who walk through *that* specific clinic door, totally missing everyone getting supplies from local chemists or private shops. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T027#GNS226_U6_T027_h7)

question: What is a common oversight that compromises infection control during busy clinic hours?

options.A: Changing examination gloves between every single patient
options.B: Rushing instrument sterilization and processing protocols
options.C: Using too much soap during routine handwashing procedures
options.D: Storing sterile medical supplies in clean cabinets

explanation: You got it! When the clinic gets busy, rushing the autoclaving or cleaning of instruments can leave germs behind and spread infections. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T4#GNS312_U5_T4_h5)

question: A conscious patient refuses to take their prescribed medication. What should you do first?

options.A: Threaten to discharge them immediately from the ward
options.B: Crush the drug into their food without telling them
options.C: Force the medication into their mouth for their own good
options.D: Explore their reasons and notify the prescriber

explanation: Patients always have the right to say no. Take a moment to listen to their worries and let the doctor know, rather than forcing anything. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T1#GNS125_U3_T1_h4)

question: What does the intravenous route involve delivering substances directly into?

options.A: Muscle tissue for slow absorption
options.B: Fatty tissue beneath the skin
options.C: Systemic circulation through a vein
options.D: The digestive tract via the stomach

explanation: Intravenous means inside a vein, allowing direct delivery into the bloodstream for rapid effect. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h1)

question: What vital information must go on the label of a freshly diluted lotion?

options.A: New concentration and expiration date
options.B: The name of the pharmacy technician who delivered it
options.C: The manufacturer's original batch number only
options.D: The patient's room number and diagnosis

explanation: Always label the new strength and expiry date so no one accidentally applies the wrong dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h6)

question: What is the primary function of synovial fluid inside a joint capsule?

options.A: Fighting off systemic blood infections
options.B: Producing red blood cells for the limb
options.C: Anchoring muscles firmly to the bone
options.D: Lubricating the joint and nourishing cartilage

explanation: Synovial fluid acts as a natural shock absorber and lubricant while feeding the joint cartilage. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T9#GNS125_U3_T9_h2)

question: A survivor states she does not want to report her assault to the police right now. What is the appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Respect her decision while providing medical care and safety planning
options.B: Refuse to treat her injuries until she agrees to press charges
options.C: Call the police immediately behind her back to ensure justice
options.D: Scold her for protecting the person who hurt her

explanation: Forcing legal reporting strips away the patient's autonomy; honoring their pace builds trust and safety. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T12#GNS312_U4_T12_h6)

question: In the PQRST pain assessment tool, what does the letter 'Q' stand for?

options.A: Quietness
options.B: Quickness
options.C: Quality
options.D: Quantity

explanation: Great job! 'Q' stands for Quality. It means asking the patient to describe what the pain feels like—is it sharp, dull, stabbing, or throbbing? [learn more](GNS123_U2_T1#GNS123_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which of these is a major physical trigger that can push a mum into distress during labour?

options.A: High pre-pregnancy weight
options.B: Early rupture of membranes
options.C: Prolonged labour
options.D: Low maternal height

explanation: When labour goes on for too long, a mum's physical and emotional energy tanks are bound to empty out, leading straight to distress. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h3)

question: What blood glucose level is generally used to define hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) in clinical practice?

options.A: Above 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
options.B: Below 6.0 mmol/L (108 mg/dL)
options.C: Below 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL)
options.D: Above 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)

explanation: Spot on! Any reading under 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) means the blood sugar is too low and the patient needs help quickly. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h6)

question: Why do single neurons connect with hundreds of other neurons instead of working totally alone?

options.A: To prevent the spread of harmful electrical storms in the spinal cord
options.B: To ensure that sensory messages never reach the motor cortex
options.C: To slow down electrical signals so the brain can rest between tasks
options.D: To allow the body to process simple reflexes and complex thoughts simultaneously

explanation: Neurons love teamwork! By linking up in networks, they help your brain multitask effortlessly—handling quick reflexes and deep thoughts all at once. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h1)

question: What does 'parenteral route' mean when talking about how diseases spread?

options.A: Entry through a break in the skin via needles or sharps
options.B: Inhalation of airborne droplets through the nose
options.C: Ingestion of contaminated food or drinking water
options.D: Spread through direct skin-to-skin physical contact

explanation: Think of parenteral as bypassing the skin barrier completely—usually when a contaminated needle or sharp punctures the tissue directly. Simple and clear! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h2)

question: When does tertiary prevention happen along the care continuum?

options.A: After a diagnosis and treatment have already occurred
options.B: While administering vaccines in a community health clinic
options.C: During routine screening tests for healthy people
options.D: Before any exposure to environmental toxins happens

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after treatment to help patients recover, manage long-term effects, and get back to daily life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why do doctors often prescribe hormonal contraceptives for women with oligomenorrhoea?

options.A: To induce regular withdrawal bleeding and protect the uterine lining
options.B: To permanently stop the natural production of all body hormones
options.C: To permanently cure the underlying genetic defect in the ovaries
options.D: To stimulate the immediate release of multiple eggs every month

explanation: Spot on! Contraceptives help shed the uterine lining on a regular schedule, preventing it from building up too much when natural ovulation isn't happening. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T5#GNS216_U2_T5_h5)

question: A community health nurse conducts a household survey to count active tuberculosis cases. What type of data is this primarily?

options.A: Hypothetical data
options.B: Quantitative data
options.C: Secondary data
options.D: Qualitative data

explanation: Counting active cases involves numerical measurements, which classifies the information as quantitative data. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h2)

question: What are the standard cardinal signs evaluated during a routine physical assessment?

options.A: Temperature, pulse, respiration, and blood pressure
options.B: Pain level, reflex response, pupil size, and skin color
options.C: Mental status, urine output, bowel sounds, and core temperature
options.D: Weight, height, blood glucose, and visual acuity

explanation: The four classic cardinal vital signs reflect the most critical life-sustaining physiological functions of the body. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h1)

question: How can a nurse help a client who is struggling with transportation to a clinic appointment?

options.A: Connecting her with affordable clinic options or community support
options.B: Telling her that missing the appointment has no health consequences
options.C: Insisting that she buy a personal vehicle before discharge
options.D: Advising her to walk several miles alone in the hot afternoon sun

explanation: Practical problems like transport can stop mums from getting care. Helping them find nearby or affordable options makes a huge difference. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T023#GNS226_U3_T023_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of advance care planning?

options.A: To ensure patient wishes guide future treatment
options.B: To let healthcare providers make all choices
options.C: To speed up the legal probate process
options.D: To reduce hospital cleaning costs

explanation: Spot on! Advance care planning makes sure the patient's voice is heard and respected, even if they can no longer speak for themselves later on. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T3#GNS321_U4_T3_h4)

question: Which medication class is widely known to cause constipation as a side effect?

options.A: Short-acting diuretics
options.B: Opioid pain relievers
options.C: Inhaled bronchodilators
options.D: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Opioids slow down gastrointestinal motility significantly, which frequently leads to stubborn constipation in patients taking them. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h2)

question: Why do healthcare decisions often involve political negotiation?

options.A: Medical equipment never breaks down unexpectedly
options.B: Resources are limited and demand is high
options.C: Doctors refuse to speak with government officials
options.D: Patients prefer traditional healers to hospitals

explanation: Scarcity forces leaders to make tough choices about where money and support go, which requires political bargaining. [learn more](GST321_U6_T3#GST321_U6_T3_h1)

question: Which task is usually handled by the circulating nurse?

options.A: Scrubbing up and handing instruments to the surgeon
options.B: Performing the actual surgical incision on the patient
options.C: Managing the patient's airway and breathing tubes
options.D: Opening sterile packages and managing room equipment

explanation: The circulating nurse is unsterile and moves freely around the room to open supplies, manage equipment, and help the team with whatever they need. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T13#GNS123_U5_T13_h5)

question: Why is cellular differentiation so important for the human body?

options.A: It ensures that all cells in the body remain identical
options.B: It stops normal cells from resting
options.C: It allows basic cells to mature into specific functional cells
options.D: It keeps the immune system calm

explanation: Brilliant! Differentiation is how a simple stem cell becomes a specialized muscle, nerve, or blood cell to do specific jobs in the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)
